h1: Beer with paneer dishes from tikka to palak paneer
title: Beer with Paneer Tikka and Palak Paneer | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer pairings for paneer tikka, palak paneer, paneer butter masala, kadai paneer and shahi paneer, with the beer style that suits each dish.
teaser: Paneer is mild, so the sauce decides the beer. Here is the right pour for tikka, palak, makhani and kadai.
standfirst: Paneer itself tastes of fresh milk and very little else. What you pair with is the marinade, the gravy or the char from the tandoor. Here is how we would match beer to the most popular paneer dishes.
sections:
Paneer is a fresh cheese made by curdling hot milk with an acid such as lemon juice or vinegar, then pressing the curds. It is not aged, so it has none of the sharp, salty flavours of cheddar or parmesan. It is mild, milky and firm. It also does not melt.

That makes paneer pairing simple: look past the cheese to the cooking. A charred tikka, a creamy makhani gravy and an earthy spinach sauce each want a different beer. Paneer's own richness, from milk fat, is the one constant. Carbonation helps with that every time.
Paneer tikka loves a toasty lager

Paneer tikka is marinated in yoghurt, ginger, garlic, chilli and spices, then cooked in a tandoor or under a grill until the edges char. That char is the key flavour.

A Vienna lager or a Märzen is our first choice. Toasted, lightly caramel malt meets the char without competing, while 18 to 25 IBU gives enough bitterness to cut the yoghurt marinade. A Pilsner works too if you want something crisper. If you like dark beer, a schwarzbier at about 5% ABV is a clever match: roasty but light bodied, so it echoes the tandoor without feeling heavy.

Palak paneer is paneer in a smooth spinach gravy with garlic, ginger and often a little cream. It is earthy, green and mild.

Spinach can taste metallic beside very bitter or roasty beers. A Helles, soft and bready at 16 to 22 IBU, is a gentle, safe match. A Belgian witbier is our favourite: the wheat body matches the creaminess, while its coriander and orange peel brighten the greens. Saag paneer and methi paneer follow the same logic, though methi's bitterness makes the softer Helles a better bet.
Paneer butter masala and shahi paneer need bubbles

Paneer butter masala, also called paneer makhani, is paneer in a tomato, butter and cream gravy with kasuri methi. Shahi paneer goes richer still with cashew, cream and sometimes saffron. These are sweet, rich and only mildly spiced.

Here carbonation does the heavy lifting. A Pilsner, a Kölsch or a crisp pale lager cleans butter and cream off the palate. A Belgian tripel, highly carbonated with a dry finish, is a bold option for shahi paneer, but at 7.5 to 9.5% ABV it should be a small glass. Our guide to beer with butter chicken and dal makhani covers the same family of gravies.

One caution with the sweeter gravies. Many restaurant makhani sauces have sugar or honey added. Sweetness in food makes beer taste drier and more bitter than it is. A Pilsner that is perfectly balanced on its own can taste sharp next to a very sweet paneer butter masala. If that happens, move to a beer with a little more malt, such as a Helles or a Vienna lager. It is a small switch that makes a big difference.
Kadai paneer and chilli paneer bring the heat

Kadai paneer is cooked with capsicum, onion and a freshly ground spice mix of coriander seed and dry red chilli. Chilli paneer, the Indo-Chinese favourite, is tossed with soy, vinegar, green chilli and spring onion.

With more chilli in play, keep bitterness down. A hefeweizen is excellent with chilli paneer, its soft wheat calming the heat. For kadai paneer, an amber lager matches the roasted spice and the capsicum. Avoid strong IPAs here. High bitterness plus chilli makes the heat linger longer than it should.

Paneer bhurji, the scrambled paneer with onion, tomato and green chilli, sits between the two. It is quick, savoury and mildly hot. A Kölsch or a pale lager is all it needs, especially as a late night snack with pav.
Matching beer to paneer at a party

Paneer is often the vegetarian centrepiece at Indian gatherings. If you are planning beer for a mixed crowd, three styles cover almost every paneer dish: a Pilsner for the creamy gravies, a witbier for spinach and herbs and a Vienna or amber lager for tikka and kadai. Serve the lagers at 4 to 7 °C and the witbier at 6 to 8 °C.

Offer something for guests who do not drink, like a fresh lime soda. Put out water too. For more on matching beer across a whole Indian menu, see our Indian food and beer pairing guide.
Taste the sauce, not the cheese

Here is a quick experiment. Take plain paneer cubes, a spoon of makhani gravy and a spoon of palak. Taste each with the same Pilsner. The plain paneer barely changes the beer. The makhani makes the beer taste more bitter. The spinach may make it taste slightly metallic. That shows you, in a minute, why the sauce decides the pairing.

Your first step: order paneer tikka and palak paneer together next time and try each with a single Pilsner. Notice how differently the same beer behaves.
faqs: What beer goes with paneer tikka?
A Vienna lager or Märzen. Toasted malt suits the tandoor char and moderate bitterness cuts the yoghurt marinade.
A Belgian witbier or a soft Helles. Avoid very bitter or roasty beers, which can taste metallic with spinach.
What beer pairs with paneer butter masala?
A crisp Pilsner, Kölsch or pale lager. High carbonation clears the butter and cream from your palate between bites.
